lessons.title: What coaching is and when to use it
lessons.html:
Coaching on the farm

On-the-job coaching is a structured way of helping a person improve their performance in their real work, at the real workplace, with a coach who guides, demonstrates, observes and gives feedback. It differs from classroom training because the learner practises with the actual tractor, dairy parlour, packshed line or spray rig they use every day.

Coaching, training and mentoring

MethodFocus
TrainingTeaching new knowledge and skills, often to groups
CoachingImproving performance in specific tasks, short to medium term
MentoringLong-term career and personal development guided by an experienced person

When coaching is the right tool

  • A new milker knows the steps from induction but still strips cows poorly and somatic cell counts are rising.
  • A tractor driver has been promoted to operate the planter and must learn calibration.
  • An extension officer wants a lead farmer to run study-group meetings on their own.
  • A worker's performance has dropped and the reason is a skill gap, not a disciplinary matter.

Coaching is not the answer when the problem is caused by broken equipment, unclear instructions, lack of materials or a personal or disciplinary issue. Find the real cause before you coach.

Qualities of a good coach

  • Knows the task well and can demonstrate it correctly and safely.
  • Listens more than talks and asks open questions.
  • Is patient, respectful and encourages questions in the learner's own language where possible.
  • Gives honest, specific feedback without humiliating anyone, never in front of the team to embarrass them.
  • Keeps promises and follows up.

Remember that adults learn best when they see why the skill matters to them, can build on what they already know and get to practise soon after being shown.

lessons.title: Planning and preparing a coaching session
lessons.html:
Preparing to coach

Good coaching is planned. Start by agreeing with the learner and their supervisor what the gap is and what good performance looks like.

Step 1: Identify the need

Use evidence: production records, quality reports, observation and the learner's own view. For example, a planter operator's rows show skips and doubles, and the plant population count is below target.

Step 2: Set clear outcomes

Write what the learner will be able to do after coaching, and to what standard. Example: the operator will calibrate the planter for the seed and spacing on the planting instruction and achieve the target seed count over a measured distance without supervision.

Step 3: Break the task into steps

Do a simple task breakdown: list each step, the key point for each (what makes it right) and the safety points. This becomes your coaching guide and later a checklist.

Step 4: Plan the practicalities

  • Time and place that does not clash with peak work, for example before planting starts rather than in the middle of a planting day.
  • Equipment, materials and protective clothing needed.
  • Safety: lock-out of machinery during adjustments, PPE, first aider available. The OHS Act 85 of 1993 requires the employer to provide training and supervision so that work is done safely.
  • Language and literacy: plan to use pictures, demonstration and the learner's home language if needed.

Step 5: Agree a coaching plan

A short written plan records the outcomes, sessions, dates and how progress will be checked. Share it with the learner so they know what to expect. Coaching works best as several short sessions with practice in between, not one long lecture.

Prepare the learner

Explain the purpose, reassure them that coaching is support, not punishment, and find out what they already know. Ask them how they prefer to learn: some want to watch first, others want to try straight away.

lessons.title: Running the session, giving feedback and evaluating
lessons.html:
The coaching cycle

A simple and reliable method is tell, show, do, review.

  1. Tell: explain the purpose of the task and the main steps in plain words.
  2. Show: demonstrate at normal speed, then slowly, stressing key points and safety points.
  3. Do: let the learner perform the task while you watch. Let them talk you through what they are doing. Step in immediately only if there is a safety risk or damage to equipment or animals.
  4. Review: discuss together what went well and what to improve, then practise again.

Asking good questions

Open questions make the learner think: What do you check before you start? What would happen if the seed plate is wrong? How will you know the setting is right? Avoid questions that only need yes or no.

Giving feedback

  • Be specific: say exactly what was done, not general praise or criticism.
  • Start with what was done well, then one or two points to improve, then encouragement.
  • Focus on the behaviour, not the person.
  • Give feedback soon after the task, in private if it is corrective.
  • Check understanding by asking the learner to summarise what they will do next time.

Evaluating progress

Use the task breakdown as a checklist and observe the learner doing the job on their own. Compare with the outcome agreed at the start: target seed count reached, cell counts falling, rows straight. Ask the learner how confident they feel. If the standard is not yet met, agree further practice; if it is met, record it.

Recording and follow-up

Keep a coaching record with dates, what was covered, progress and sign-off by learner and coach. Records support skills development reporting and help when the worker is assessed formally against a unit standard. Follow up after a few weeks to check the skill has stuck, and recognise the improvement.

Key points

  • Coaching improves performance in real tasks at the real workplace.
  • Find the real cause of a performance gap before deciding to coach.
  • Plan outcomes, task steps, safety and practicalities in advance.
  • Use tell, show, do, review and ask open questions.
  • Give specific, timely, private feedback and record progress.

quiz.question: What makes on-the-job coaching different from classroom training?

options.text: It is always done in groups
The learner practises with the real equipment at the real workplace

quiz.question: A worker performs badly because the pump is broken. What should you do?

options.text: Fix the real cause, the equipment, because coaching will not solve it

quiz.question: What is the correct order of the coaching cycle described in the lessons?

options.text: How will you know the setting is right?

quiz.question: When should a coach step in immediately while the learner is doing the task?

options.text: Whenever the learner is slower than the coach
When there is a safety risk or damage to equipment or animals
Only at the end of the day

quiz.question: Corrective feedback is best given in front of the whole team so that everyone learns.
A task breakdown lists each step, its key points and the safety points, and can later be used as a checklist.
Which describe good feedback? (select all that apply)

options.text: Focused on the behaviour, not the person
Ends with checking the learner understands what to do next time
